content.text:
Operator
Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Q2 2024 Comfort Systems USA Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speaker's presentation, there will be a question and answer session. To ask a question during the session, you will need to press star one one on your telephone. You will then hear an automated message advising your hand is raised. To withdraw your question, please press star one one again. Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your speaker today, Julie Shaeff, Chief Accounting Officer. Please go ahead.
Julie S. Shaeff
SVP and Chief Accounting Officer, Comfort Systems USA
Thanks, Daniel. Good morning. Welcome to Comfort Systems USA's Q2 2024 Earnings Call. Our comments today, as well as our press releases, contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the applicable securities laws and regulations. What we will say today is based upon the current plans and expectations of Comfort Systems USA. Those plans and expectations include risks and uncertainties that might cause actual future activities and results of our operations to be materially different from those set forth in our comments. You can read a detailed listing and commentary concerning our specific risk factors in our most recent Form 10-K and Form 10-Q, as well as in our press release covering these earnings. A slide presentation is provided as a companion to our remarks and is posted on the investor relations section of the company's website, found at comfortsystemsusa.com.
Joining me on the call today are Brian Lane, President and Chief Executive Officer, Trent McKenna, Chief Operating Officer, and Bill George, Chief Financial Officer. Brian will open our remarks.
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Okay, thanks, Julie. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us on the call today. We had a fantastic quarter as our teams achieved superb execution for our customers. We earned $3.74 per share this quarter, which is an increase of over 90% compared to a year ago. Our mechanical business exceeded last year and our electrical segment achieved unprecedented margins. Both operating income and EBITDA dollars increased by 100% this quarter compared to 2023. Demand remains strong, especially in the industrial sector, including technology and other manufacturing customers. Our backlog continues to track at high levels despite our strong revenue for the quarter. Backlog is $5.8 billion, far higher on both an absolute and a same-store basis than this time last year.
We continue to select work that has good margins and good working conditions for our valuable people. I will discuss our business and outlook in a few minutes, but first I will turn this call over to Bill to review our financial performance. Bill?
Bill George
EVP and CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Thanks, Brian. Q2 results were really remarkable. We had 30% same-store revenue growth, higher margins, good SG&A leverage, and over $165 million in free cash flow. We achieved more than $200 million in quarterly EBITDA for the first time, and our EBITDA doubled compared to the same quarter last year. Revenue for Q2 2024 was $1.8 billion, and that is an increase of $514 million or 40% compared to last year. Our Mechanical segment revenue increased by 49%, benefiting from organic construction and service growth, recent acquisitions, and modular expansion. Electrical segment revenue increased by 12% and overall our same-store revenue increased by 30% or $383 million, with the remaining $131 million of increase resulting from acquisitions.
We are facing tougher prior year comparable results for the remainder of the year. Through H1, our same-store revenue growth has been 26%. Currently, our best estimate is that for full year 2024, our same-store revenue growth will be in the low to mid-20% range. Gross profit was $364 million for Q2 2024, a noteworthy $136 million improvement compared to a year ago. Our gross profit percentage grew to 20.1% this quarter, compared to 17.6% for Q2 2023. Quarterly gross profit percentage in our electrical segment jumped to 23.6% this year as compared to 17% last year.
Margins in our mechanical segment also increased significantly to 19.2% as compared to 17.8% in Q2 2023. EBITDA doubled to $223 million this quarter from a strong $112 million in Q2 2023. Same-store EBITDA increased by over 80%, and even without recent acquisitions, our EBITDA exceeded $200 million. Considering the strong ongoing demand, we expect that for 2024, EBITDA margins will continue in the strong ranges that we have achieved over the last several quarters. SG&A expense for the quarter was $180 million or 9.9% of revenue, compared to $136 million or 10.5% of revenue in Q2 2023.
Our operating income increased by just over 100% from last year, from $92 million in Q2 2023 to $185 million for Q2 2024. With improved gross profit margins and favorable SG&A leverage, our operating income percentage surged to 10.2% this quarter from 7.1% in the prior year. This is the first time that we have achieved 10% OI margins in a quarter. Since I became CFO, Comfort Systems has not used adjusted numbers to make our results look better. However, today I do wanna point out a notable factor in our results. Our recent acquisitions have exceeded our high expectations, resulting in larger than usual earn out expense. Without the changes in the fair value of our earn out obligations this quarter, certain earnings would have been notably stronger.
We always have purchase-related adjustments in the periods following an acquisition. However, they currently are and likely will continue to be much larger over the next several quarters because of the significant contingent consideration opportunity included in recent transactions. Our year-to-date tax rate was 21.3%. We currently estimate that the full year 2024 tax rate will likely be in the 21% to 22% range. After considering all of these factors, net income for Q2 2024 was $134 million or $3.74 per share. This is a 90% improvement from last year. Free cash flow for H1 2024 was $290 million. We continue to benefit from advanced payments for work that we will fund and complete in upcoming quarters.
Operating cash flow continues to exceed our earnings by about $300 million on a trailing twelve-month basis. We are well ahead of earnings in collecting our cash. Even with two notable acquisitions earlier this year, we have succeeded in retiring all of our bank debt as of 30 June 2024, and other debt was $91 million with cash balances exceeding our debt. We also spent around $11 million on share repurchases this quarter. That's what I got, Brian.
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Okay. Thanks, Bill. I'm going to discuss our business and outlook. Our backlog at the end of Q2 was $5.8 billion, a large year-over-year increase and a modest sequential decline. Since last year, our backlog has increased by $1.6 billion or 38%. $1 billion of the increase was same-store, and $0.6 billion was new backlog from recent acquisitions. We are entering H2 2024 with 25% more same-store backlog than we had at this time last year, despite a roughly 30% surge in organic revenue. Our revenue mix continues to trend towards data centers, chip fab, battery plants, life science, and food.
Industrial customers accounted for 60% of total revenue in H1 2024, and they are major drivers of pipeline and backlog. Technology, which is included in industrial, was 31% of our revenue, a substantial increase from 20% the prior year. Institutional markets, which include education, healthcare, and government, are also strong and represent 23% of our revenue. The commercial sector remains reasonably active in the regions that we serve, but it is now a smaller part of our business at about 17% of revenue. Most of our service revenue is for commercial customers, so the share of our construction revenue that is commercial is now relatively small. Construction activities continue to be extraordinarily strong, and our project pipelines continue at unprecedented high levels.
Construction accounted for 84% of our revenue, with projects for new buildings representing 59% and existing building construction 25%. We include modular in new building construction, and year-to-date modular was 18% of our revenue. Service revenue was 16% of our total revenue, as our service revenue increased by 10% and service profit grew by 20% this quarter. Service is a reliable source of profit and cash flow and is on track to exceed $1 billion in revenue for 2024. We are entering H2 2024 with a backlog that is 25% higher on a same-store basis than we had at this time last year, and we have a superb team working hard for our customers every single day.
Thanks to the dedication and hard work of our employees across the country, we are optimistic about our future. As always, I want to close by thanking our over 17,000 employees for their hard work and dedication. I will now turn it back over to Daniel for questions. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. As a reminder, to ask a question, please press star one one on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press star one one again. Please stand by while we compile the Q&A roster. Our first question comes from Alex Dwyer with KeyBanc Capital Markets. Your line is now open.
Alex Dwyer
Associate and Equity Research, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Hey, good morning. Thanks for taking my question.
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Morning.
Alex Dwyer
Associate and Equity Research, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Morning. So it's nice to see the continued strength in margins and the guidance calls for this to continue this year. How sustainable do you think these margins are as we think about the business on a longer-term basis? Is there any reason to think these margins would ultimately revert back more towards the historical averages over time?
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
You know, I think Alex, particularly as, you know, the upcoming short term, we're in pretty good shape to maintain these margins. We're getting good pricing, and we're getting excellent execution in the field. Also, you can't forget we are, you know, growing service 10%, and you see profitability increase there. I think we're pretty optimistic, you know, in the near future that we should maintain these margins.
Bill George
EVP and CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah, I would say every factor that is creating these margins is continuing at least as strong as it has been, and in some cases continues to get stronger.
Alex Dwyer
Associate and Equity Research, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Got it. The modular construction performance in the quarter, was most of that project activity for data centers? More broadly, how do we think about the growth algorithm in modular going forward, capacity additions and the ability for the business to gain efficiencies over time?
Bill George
EVP and CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Modular, like really every single part of our business, did great this quarter. It's, as you can see, it's growing. It's up to, you know, near 18% of our revenue. You know, it's adding a percentage while the revenue is growing very quickly. That's continued to grow. As far as the future, you know, people have been asking a lot. Are we going to make new large commitments to space? I don't think that is something that. We are taking incremental commitments. We have added incremental space within the last few months. We're more likely to do things incrementally.
I do want to say that one of the things that we emphasized when we took the additional one million sq ft of space that we took recently. We took space that had much higher roofs and was much more configured for automation. I think a lot of our goal is going to be to improve the production and productivity of the newly deployed space. Ultimately, Comfort is going to take the amount of work we can execute. You know, there are businesses that you can scale easily. This is a business that you're doing things in the real world. You're delivering things that are three stories tall and 100yd long, and they have incredible complexity inside them.
You have to respect the difficulty of what you're doing and make sure we will always put our ability to keep our promises to our customers above sort of pushing for growth on the top line. Thank you. I'll turn it over.
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Thanks.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Adam Thalhimer with Thompson Davis. Your line is now open.
Adam Thalhimer
Director of Research, Thompson Davis
Hey, good morning, guys. Great quarter.
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Hey, Adam.
Bill George
EVP and CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Hey, Adam. How you doing?
Adam Thalhimer
Director of Research, Thompson Davis
Good. All right, also on modular. I think it was late December 2022. You had, like, a program award for modular? I'm curious if you see the potential for more of those going forward or if.
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
So-
Adam Thalhimer
Director of Research, Thompson Davis
Future modular awards are more one-off.
Bill George
EVP and CFO, Comfort Systems USA
I don't know about one-off. They're just constant. In December 2021, there was a big commitment that was part of really more than a year's negotiation with a large customer that induced us to make a really big investment in one million sq ft of additional space. Since then, we have been able to keep the backlog at least the levels that we achieved, sort of in that timeframe. It's the awards sort of come in as programs are completed, right? These. There are redesigns that happen in the products that we sell.
I don't know if it will continue, but I will say in the last three years, we've tended to get more of the modular bookings in the winter months, sort of December, January, and February, and we've had sort of a net burn in the middle of the year. We certainly had a net burn in modular this Q2, but it's because we had really big bookings over the winter. I think our prospects are good for that, but obviously, it depends, you know, it depends if people are still planning on having data and computing power, right? Which we think they are.
Adam Thalhimer
Director of Research, Thompson Davis
All right. Well, that was my next question, backlog seasonality, 'cause for a couple of years now, it's been burn over the summer and build over the winter. Can that happen again?
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah. If you look at last year, we sort of went through the same cycle. I mean, the thing you look at, we look at, Adam, is, you know, what's the demand? What's our pipelines look like? You know, they're robust. It's in all the markets we served. It's probably as strong. I've been doing this for 47 years. It's probably the best market I've ever been in. You know, we're pretty optimistic. There's plenty of work for a while.
Adam Thalhimer
Director of Research, Thompson Davis
Lastly, can you just comment on Texas Electrical, the margins over 22% again for the third straight quarter? Kinda, what's the outlook for that business?
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah. Well, first of all, you know, the electrical company we have here, you know, is really a superb company that Bill found for sure. They're in the four big markets that we like in Texas. We have more electricians than anyone else, and Texas is booming. We got a lot of mission-critical work, which is really in your sweet spot. We're really humming along on that business right now, and I think it'll go on for a while.
Bill George
EVP and CFO, Comfort Systems USA
It's also important to know, it's the electrical segment is not just Texas. We have unbelievable results right now in Kentucky and North Carolina. We have just fantastic electrical businesses. People need what they do. They do a great job for their customers, and they make sure that they get paid for the capacity that they can bring to bear and for the risks that they take. It's really to hit those kinda numbers, pretty much everybody had to be just having an amazing outcome.
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
It's good to have electricians right now, Adam.
Adam Thalhimer
Director of Research, Thompson Davis
Good to hear. All right. Thank you, guys.
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
All right. Thank you.
Bill George
EVP and CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Thanks.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Josh Chan with UBS. Your line is now open.
Josh Chan
Executive Director and Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Hi. Good morning, guys. Congrats on a really good quarter.
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Thanks, Josh.
Josh Chan
Executive Director and Equity Research Analyst, UBS
I guess, Brian, if you were to look at the bidding pipeline, you know, do you see kind of new projects popping up for bid at similar or stronger rates? Where are those verticals, any difference versus sort of the recent past?
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
You know, I think, you know, if you look at the pipelines in the backlog, it's probably pretty consistent for the last, you know, 18 months to two years. We're still seeing, you know, as we mentioned in the script, similar opportunities, you know, data centers, pharma, life sciences, food, etc. We're seeing the mix pretty consistent in the markets that we serve. There's been no letup, Josh.
Bill George
EVP and CFO, Comfort Systems USA
If you don't mind, I'll just comment on.
Josh Chan
Executive Director and Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Yeah.
Bill George
EVP and CFO, Comfort Systems USA
on data centers. There are people right now who seem to be concerned that something's happening with the data center build. What we are hearing from our customers and experiencing in the market is that they are continuing to believe in deploying data centers. They've bought a lot of very, very expensive computer chips. They're taking delivery of those on a regular basis. Our understanding is they're gonna be deployed into servers and put in buildings that are gonna need to be cooled. They're gonna need to be heated. I mean, sorry, they're gonna need electricity. They'll be heated by the servers. Also, we're seeing data center work pop up in places that hasn't started yet in states where we hadn't seen data centers before.
It's possible, I guess, that that's slowing down, but I will say if that's happening, it's certainly not in anything that we can see or experience in our vision or our markets, or in our conversations with our customers.
Josh Chan
Executive Director and Equity Research Analyst, UBS
That's encouraging, and thanks for the color there. I guess in this current environment, how do you keep your employees kinda happy? I know no one is, like, relaxed working this hard, but any concerns about the sustainability of everybody working this hard for a long time?
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah. You know, Josh, that is a great question, and thanks for asking it. We really take, you know, great pride in protecting our folks from a health and safety perspective, treat them fair. We treat them with respect. We have a lot of work for them to do, which is great for themselves and their families. But at the end of the day, we are extremely grateful for the hard work and commitment they're all making. We really go out of our way. We're very field-focused in this company, which I'm really proud of, and we really do try to take care of them as best we can. They like a lot of work. They like to work. You know, we're in a good time for them as well.
Thanks. Thanks for asking.
Josh Chan
Executive Director and Equity Research Analyst, UBS
That's good. Maybe I can sneak one more in. If people were to ask you what percentage of your business do you think is exposed to AI, how would you address that? Is that the data center portion, or how would you kind of think about that?
Bill George
EVP and CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Well, you know, I think AI. Let's say the demand for data, right? Because even before the AI build really only started last year, 15 months, right? There was heavy data center construction 'cause people were getting ready for streaming. Everybody's forgotten about that. You know, compute power, the AI thing is an incremental add to what was already a very solid pipeline. I would say that it's both AI and chips that are affected by, driven by, you know, decisions by hyperscalers to protect their core businesses by making sure they're not left behind and to prepare for opportunities of the future by building out this capacity. I don't know if that helps, but.
Josh Chan
Executive Director and Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Yeah. Thanks, Bill. Thanks, thank you both for the response and the time.
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Julio Romero with Sidoti & Company. Your line is now open.
Julio Romero
Senior Equity Research Analyst, SIdoti and Company
Thanks. Hey, good morning, guys.
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Morning.
Julio Romero
Senior Equity Research Analyst, SIdoti and Company
Good morning. You guys talked about, you know, same-store sales growth in the low to mid-20% range for the full year. You know, I guess that implies at least 15%-ish growth in the H2. Just any thoughts about how we should think about same-store sales growth percentages in Q3 and then in Q4?
Bill George
EVP and CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Through 11 months, it was 26%. To sort of be the low-mid teens, it would have to come down some, but maybe not down to 15, right? If the H2 was 15, that's gonna average below 20. It's a little stronger than that. We don't really know what's gonna happen. There's a lot at stake. We are on 1 July this year, we had 25% more booked work on a same-store basis than we had last year. You know, we believe we're gonna have very strong growth for the full year. Our best estimate is that low-mid 20% range. I will say there's a range around that of what could happen. We have seemed to be surprised to the upside lately.
Julio Romero
Senior Equity Research Analyst, SIdoti and Company
Got it. That, that's helpful. Then you guys talked about factors that are creating these margins. You know, one of them I would think would be project selection. Can you maybe just talk about that and how crucial of a factor that is in creating these margins? Is that kind of like a rising tide of sorts, where you can just continue to see, you know, greater quantity of opportunities than you're able to do, and therefore you're able to become more and more selective on these projects?
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah. I think, you know, we have a process. We, you know, like most people do, go, no-go. You know, we're very careful to select where we're putting our valuable resources, you know, with good customers, you know, and doing good work. It's really important that you go through the factors in selecting, you know, what work you're gonna take in a market like this when there's a lot of work out there, Julio.
Julio Romero
Senior Equity Research Analyst, SIdoti and Company
Okay. Last one for me would just be, you know, on that 10% operating margin milestone that you hit in this quarter. I think it may also be the first time, at least in quite a while, that your SG&A margin has a nine handle on it.
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Yep.
Julio Romero
Senior Equity Research Analyst, SIdoti and Company
Maybe if you could just touch on SG&A leverage and how we should be thinking about that, going forward?
Bill George
EVP and CFO, Comfort Systems USA
It's a great question. It's gonna be hard to get much more SG&A leverage just mathematically, right? But I do think this range is we should continue in because we're continuing to get the revenue growth. You know, we did have notable dollar increases in SG&A this quarter. It does take money to do this work. I guess I would say I guess if that were a modeling question, I wouldn't count on a whole lot more leverage. I think the leverage we've gotten so far is pretty solid until revenue, you know, trends were to change. Yeah.
Julio Romero
Senior Equity Research Analyst, SIdoti and Company
Got it. I'll pass it along. Thanks very much, guys.
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Thanks.
Bill George
EVP and CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Thanks.
Operator
Thank you. I'm showing no further questions at this time. I would now like to turn it back to Brian Lane for closing remarks.
Brian E. Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
All right. Thanks everyone, you know, for listening in today. I really wanna thank our amazing employees again. We're really grateful, you know, for the work that they do. I hope everyone enjoys their summer and the weekend, and we look forward to seeing everybody on the road soon. Thank you.
Bill George
EVP and CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Thanks.
Operator
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

content.text:
Operator
Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Q1 2024 Comfort Systems USA Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are on a listen-only mode. After the speaker's presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question during the session, you'll need to press star one one on your telephone. You will then hear an automated message advising that your hand is raised. To withdraw your question, please press star one one again. Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. We would now like to hand the conference over to your speaker today, Julie Shaeff, Chief Accounting Officer. Please go ahead.
Julie Shaeff
Chief Accounting Officer, Comfort Systems USA
Thanks, Justin. Good morning. Welcome to Comfort Systems USA's Q1 2024 Earnings Call. Our comments today, as well as our press releases, contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the applicable securities laws and regulations. What we will say today is based on the current plans and expectations of Comfort Systems USA. Those plans and expectations include risks and uncertainties that might cause actual future activities and results of our operations to be materially different from those set forth in our comments. You can read a detailed listing and commentary concerning our specific risk factors in our most recent Form 10-K and Form 10-Q, as well as in our press release covering these earnings. A slide presentation has been provided as a companion to our remarks. This presentation is posted on the investor relations section of the company's website, found at comfortsystemsusa.com.
Joining me on the call today are Brian Lane, President and Chief Executive Officer, Trent McKenna, Chief Operating Officer, and Bill George, Chief Financial Officer. Brian will open our remarks.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Thanks, Julie. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us on the call today. 2024 is off to an outstanding start with strong revenue, fantastic margins, and continuing strong cash flow. Our dedicated teams across the country achieved superb execution, and I am deeply grateful for their hard work and commitment. We earned $2.69 per share this quarter compared to $1.59 a year ago. Our revenue was $1.5 billion with same-store growth of 23%. Our mechanical business exceeded last year, while our electrical segment achieved unprecedented margins. Backlog is $5.9 billion, up both year-over-year and sequentially on a same-store basis. Construction continues to thrive amid strong ongoing demand, and service is performing at high levels.
In February, we closed two substantial acquisitions, Summit Industrial and J & S Mechanical, and they, too, are off to a great start. Both of these companies are included in our mechanical segment. We also increased our dividend by 20%, adding $0.05 to reach $0.30 per share. This increase reflects our continuing strong cash flow and our commitment to reward our shareholders. I will discuss our business and outlook in a few minutes, but first, I will turn this call over to Bill to review our financial performance. Bill.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Thanks, Brian. You know, I can't help but also express my gratitude to the people who are working every day to create these amazing results. As Brian noted, revenue for Q1 2024 was $1.5 billion, and that is an increase of $362 million or 31% compared to last year. Same-store revenue increased by 23% or $266 million, with the remaining $96 million increase resulting from acquisitions. Our Mechanical segment revenue increased by 29%, and our Electrical segment revenue increased by 37%. We did not experience as much seasonality this Q1 as we have in the past, as an increasing proportion of our work is being performed in warmer climates.
Additionally, weather in our colder climates was favorable for construction this quarter, and with the strong growth in modular, more of our work is being performed under roof inside our modular plants. We are also facing tougher prior year comparable results for the remainder of this year. However, our best estimate is that we will achieve same-store percentage revenue increases in at least the mid-teens and more likely in the high teens for the full year. Gross profit was $297 million for Q1 2024, a $92 million improvement compared to a year ago. Our gross profit percentage improved to 19.3% this quarter compared to 17.5% for Q1 2023.
The quarterly gross profit percentage in our Electrical segment improved to 22.6% this year as compared to 16.1% last year. Margins in our Mechanical segment also increased in the quarter to 18.4% as compared to 17.9% in Q1 2023. Our Mechanical segment includes our modular business, which operates at lower margins than our remaining businesses. EBITDA improved markedly to $170 million this quarter from an already strong $90 million in Q1 2023. Same-store EBITDA increased by over 70%.
Although the Q1 benefited from the favorable factors I mentioned earlier, our underlying trend, and our underlying trends are strong. We expect that for 2024, EBITDA margins will continue to trend in the strong ranges that we have achieved over the last several quarters, and we are optimistic that full-year EBITDA margins in 2024 will match or exceed our high 2023 results. Gross margins should also remain strong, but gross margin percentage may be more variable in 2024 in light of the effect of amortization and certain purchase-related adjustments. SG&A expense for the quarter was $163 million or 10.6% of revenue, compared to $135 million or 11.5% of revenue in Q1 2023.
On a same-store basis, SG&A spend was $19 million higher due to ongoing investments to support our higher activity levels. Our operating income increased by 91% from last year, from $71 million in Q1 2023 to $135 million for Q1 2024. With improved gross profit margins and favorable SG&A leverage, our operating income percentage increased to 8.8% this quarter from 6.0% in the prior year. Changes in the fair value of our earn-out obligations this quarter reduced our income by $12 million, and that was caused by the variability noted earlier, and it was triggered by strong early performance at our recent acquisitions. We always have purchase-related adjustments in the periods following an acquisition.
However, they will likely be much larger over the next several quarters because of the size of the Summit and J & S acquisitions and the significant contingent consideration opportunities that were included in those transactions. Our Q1 tax rate was 21.7%. We currently estimate that the full year 2024 tax rate will likely be in the 21% to 22% range. After considering all these factors, net income for the Q1 of 2024 was $96 million or $2.69 per share. This compares to net income for the Q1 of 2023 of $57 million or $1.59 per share. Free cash flow for the Q1 of 2024 was $123 million.
We continue to benefit from advanced payments for work that we will fund and complete in upcoming quarters, and operating cash flow continues to exceed our earnings by about $300 million on a trailing twelve-month basis. Over the coming quarters, we expect that eventually pre-bookings and equipment advances will normalize, creating some cash flow headwind. In the meantime, these collections have allowed us to invest in growth and fund acquisitions from current cash flows while lowering interest costs. Our total debt as of 31 March 2024, was $90 million, with no funded debt from our banks, and that was despite large cash payments for the Summit and J&S acquisitions in February. As Brian noted, we also increased our dividend. Before I close, I want to mention one additional item, which is not directly relevant to our financial results, but that I wanted to flag for awareness.
Last night, a Texas jury returned a jury verdict against one of our subsidiaries relating to a 2019 safety incident. The jury verdict was over $70 million, and that pencils out to about $48 million for us. Assuming this jury's verdict is entered by the judge, we will pursue a number of strong appeals. Even if the appeals are unsuccessful, this event is not expected to have an impact on us financially. That's all I have, Brian.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
All right. Thanks, Bill. I'm going to discuss our business and outlook. Our backlog at the end of Q1 was a record $5.9 billion. Since last year, our backlog has increased by $1.5 billion or 33%, and about half of that increase was same-store growth and the other half was new backlog from companies we acquired. Our sequential backlog increased by $754 million, of which $612 million related to acquisitions. Our same-store sequential backlog increased by $142 million, and pipelines remain strong. Our revenue mix continues to trend towards data centers, chip fabrication, battery plants, life science, and food. Industrial customers accounted for 60% of total revenue in Q1, and they are major drivers of pipeline and backlog.
Technology, which is included in industrial, was 30% of our revenue, a substantial increase from 19% the prior year. Institutional markets, which include education, healthcare, and government, are also strong and represent 23% of our revenue. The commercial sector remains reasonably active in the regions that we serve, but it is now part, a smaller part of our business at about 17% of revenue. The majority of our service revenue is for commercial customers, so the share of our overall construction revenue from commercial has become relatively small. Construction grew quickly and drove great results for us this quarter. Overall, construction accounted for 84% of our revenue, with projects for new buildings representing 59% and existing building construction, 25%. We include modular and new building construction. In modular, this quarter was 16% of our revenue.
Service revenue increased this quarter, but because of the growth in construction, even with a service revenue increase, service fell to 16% of total revenue. Service, which remains seasonal, continues to be a great source of profit and cash flow for us. Comfort Systems USA is thriving, and our team members across the country are delivering exceptional results. Thanks to their excellence, and in light of the strong ongoing demand, we are optimistic that we will continue to achieve strong results in 2024. Safety, execution, and innovation remain at the forefront of our operations. We believe that our commitment to our employees and to building legacies is the foundation of our success. Our number one priority is to preserve and grow the best workforce in our industry.
As always, I wanna close by thanking our over 16,500 employees for their hard work and dedication. I will now turn it back over to Justin for questions. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. As a reminder to ask a question please press star one one on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question please press star one one again. Please standby as we compile the Q&A roster. One moment for our first question. Our first question comes from Alex Dwyer from KeyBanc Capital Markets. Your line is now open.
Alex Dwyer
Equity Research Associate, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Hi, team. Congrats on a strong start to the year.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Hi, Alex.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Hey, Alex. Thank you.
Alex Dwyer
Equity Research Associate, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Yep. The EBITDA margin was very strong this quarter, and the guide for this year continues to call for similar to last year. Can you just talk about the potential for margin expansion over the rest of the year? Is it just that the comps get tougher in the back half, or is there something in the recent performance that, like, isn't sustainable as we progress through this year?
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Well, you know, as is Brian, I'll go first and then Bill can follow up. I mean, we're really pleased with the margins that we have right now. You know, if you're in that gross margin 18% to 20% range, I think you're executing at a high level. We're over at 19% for the quarter. I think we're gonna continue to be in that range throughout the year. You know, we'll have broad-based excellent performance across our operating companies. I mean, might have a little fluctuation up and down as we go, but in general, you know, our performance has just been excellent.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah. Like as we noted in the opening comments, we're definitely anticipating, expecting our EBITDA margins for the full year to stay up near the last year, right? The recent amazing results we have, and we're optimistic we could do a little better. I will say, as you pointed out, later this year, we hit some very tough comparables, right? We had extraordinary growth and increases really progressively throughout the year and especially in the H2 last year. One of the things you're seeing is, even though last year, the Q1 seemed like extraordinary quarter, and it was, it got so much better later in the year that we're just facing tougher comparables. We're extremely optimistic, but they are tough comparables and, you know, that's why we're giving that guidance.
Alex Dwyer
Equity Research Associate, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Thank you. The organic backlog growth was very strong this quarter. Can you talk about what end markets drove that strength and if there was any, like, larger modular orders in there? Do you think it's fair to assume, like, backlog can continue to increase sequentially through this year?
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
I mean, you know, in terms of the backlog, it's broad-based. We didn't get, you know, one surge from any particular segment. It's, you know, it's really reassuring to us here. You see multisectors, particularly if you're talking about, you know, the tech sector, manufacturing, you know, education, I think at the university level, strong in healthcare, both outpatient or hospital. We're seeing good balance, you know, across the board.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah. You know, as far as what might happen in the coming quarters, it would actually surprise me at some point not to see some sequential declines, right? You can't especially as we get into the summer and the revenues get really big. Historically, we've always had sequential declines in the middle of the year, except for lately. I've been like I said, it would surprise me, but to be fair, I have been surprised quarter-after-quarter for the last several quarters. The demand is unmatched. There's never been more demand for our services, and our guys are turning away work. At some point, you can only take so much work. I think you'll see backlogs stay at extremely high levels. I don't think you should say, "Oh, yeah, for sure every sequential compare will be up." That's really not historically what happens.
Alex Dwyer
Equity Research Associate, KeyBanc Capital Markets
A last one from me. The Summit and J & S acquisitions are off to a strong start this year. Is there anything different about the integration of them into your business, given these are so large? Can you talk about the appetite for more deals through the year?
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
You know, I'll just start on the integration. You know, they are large. One a little bit of advantage you have when they're large is they get a little bit more horsepower, you know, in the back office to handle public company requirements. These are both very sophisticated companies, excellent workforce, great leadership. We're working pretty, you know, pretty closely with them to make this as smooth as possible. You know, plus they got a great attitude, you know, and integrate themselves, which is a huge help. You know, so far off to a great start.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah, I couldn't agree more. For us, integration, the biggest thing we try to do in integration is keep what's great about a company and keep it going and keep it, you know, that local excellence continuing. That's an advantage we have since we're not trying to change things. That makes integration a little easier.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
So.
Alex Dwyer
Equity Research Associate, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Thank you. I'll turn it over.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
All right.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Thank you.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. One moment for our next question. Our next question comes from Adam Thalhimer from Thompson Davis. Your line is now open.
Adam Thalhimer
Director of Research and Partner, Thompson Davis
Hey, good morning, guys. Great quarter.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Hey, thanks, Adam. Good morning.
Adam Thalhimer
Director of Research and Partner, Thompson Davis
I wanted to stick on Summit and just see kind of what you're seeing so far, specifically from chip plants, kind of the timing of those projects.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
You know, they have great work going on and great prospects. They also have a big solar fab. You know, these guys, they're perfect to do the big, hard work that the country needs right now. That's why we were so excited to buy them. Right now, it's full speed ahead.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah. You know, Adam, in terms of their skill set, you know, they're looking at a lot of opportunities in pharmaceuticals, et cetera. You know, their skills are applicable to a whole bunch of industries.
Adam Thalhimer
Director of Research and Partner, Thompson Davis
Oh, okay.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah.
Adam Thalhimer
Director of Research and Partner, Thompson Davis
What kind of capacity growth potential do they have as you start to get them more into markets?
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
You know, when we buy a company, we don't push them to grow. You know, we basically push them to grow their workforce, to really, really put their arms around and grow their workforce, which leads to growth in almost every case. But I would not say for us that's a growth story. I think like almost any company we buy, they will grow over time. But for us, it's just an excellence story. You know, keep your-
Adam Thalhimer
Director of Research and Partner, Thompson Davis
Okay.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Keep your workforce busy.
Adam Thalhimer
Director of Research and Partner, Thompson Davis
I wanted to ask about specialty contractor capacity. Is it still, do you think, as tight now as it was kind of a year or two ago? Are you still booking work further out?
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah, you know, Adam, for sure, you know, it's still tight. We've been very fortunate to recruit some outstanding people on the human resource side. We're attracting some great talent, but it is still tight. We're, you know, we're a good place to work. We offer great compensation package, the opportunity to develop. We like to promote from within. I think that'll be a struggle for a while, but we have good work. People like working here, you know, so I'm very optimistic, you know, about the future.
Adam Thalhimer
Director of Research and Partner, Thompson Davis
All right. Bill, just a quick modeling thing. What do you have for D&A in Q2, since we only had the acquisitions for part of Q1?
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
We had two months of those guys. I think it's in the footnotes. If you look in the footnotes, we actually have a table where we tell you exactly, well, almost exactly what we think it's gonna be. Just you can go get the actual numbers from one of the footnotes.
Adam Thalhimer
Director of Research and Partner, Thompson Davis
I was being lazy. Okay, thanks.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah, well.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Be honest, Adam.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
I'm being lazy too. Because I'd have to go look it up myself. It's big. It's like you saw the pop, right? That was only two months of those guys. You know, you're only required to publish that schedule once a year, but we publish it. We certainly publish it every quarter after we do an acquisition because, you know, those non-cash charges, it's crazy that we reduce our earnings by that, right? People wanna know what the asset they own is doing, but GAAP is GAAP, and so that's what we do.
Adam Thalhimer
Director of Research and Partner, Thompson Davis
Sounds good. Thank you, Bill.
Operator
Thank you. One moment for our next question. Our next question comes from Josh Chan from UBS. Your line is now open.
Josh Chan
Director and Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Hey, good morning, guys. Congrats on a really good quarter.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Thanks, Josh.
Josh Chan
Director and Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Could you talk about the bidding environment for potential projects that even are before backlogs, you know? Anything changing there, and how's pricing on those bids that you're putting together?
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah. You know, in terms of the pipeline pre-order, it's still very robust. It's still broad-based. Pricing is still reasonable for sure. It's a great opportunity for us, you know, to work for our really good customers, be very selective in the acquisition process. You know, we don't chase revenue, chasing the opportunities and the work that we're good at. In terms of the sectors that, you know, that I hit on before, the opportunities are very consistent, still today.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
No letup.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
No letup.
Josh Chan
Director and Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Okay. That's great to hear. On the data center side, could you just talk about how your conversations are like with your data center customers and any kind of update in terms of your thinking on when you might be able to expand modular capacity again?
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
You know, these are big organizations, so you're not just talking to one part of the organization, right? You're talking to the people who desperately need the capacity and who understand, you know, how to partner with us, and you're also talking to parts of the organizations whose job it is to purchase things and to try to get the lowest price. I would say that things are as expected. You know, what we try to do is just be a great partner for people. If really we do our best work and get the best value for people who reciprocate that. I don't know that anything's changed, you know. Essentially they are in an all paths to market mindset, so they love getting this stuff built modularly.
They're busy hiring our contractors who build it in the traditional way. I just think that the demand is so great that they're, you know, they're just looking for people who can help them do what they need to do, and we love to do that for people who wanna partner up.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
You know, Josh, I just add on a little bit to the opportunities. You know, one of our strengths is the size of the company and the geographic spread we have. You know, opportunity to share labor. It's really an advantage that us and a few of our colleagues throughout the country have to get some of these larger opportunities that we can handle both financially and from a resource basis. Including when you think about our suppliers, you know, we're a good company to do business with. Our size right now is really helping us.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
You know, we use that size to be a partner to people. We don't try to use it against people.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Right.
Josh Chan
Director and Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Yeah. Any thoughts on, you know, whether you could expand capacity at some time later this year or into next year?
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
If you're talking about modular, I would say that is not something that we are currently making plans around, but we are evaluating.
Josh Chan
Director and Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Okay. All right. Just a modeling question. EBITDA margins usually go up from Q1 to Q2. I know, Bill, you mentioned the lack of seasonality in Q1, but I was just wondering your thoughts about whether you can see a typical sequential margin expansion into next quarters.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah. EBITDA margins do typically go up from Q1 to Q2. Q1s have never been all-time highs by extraordinary amounts. It's a very insecure time for us to start saying we're gonna have sequential upticks in margins, and only because of how high they are in Q1. I'm more comfortable talking about doing better this year than last year, right?
Josh Chan
Director and Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Okay.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
This is a quarter where our EBITDA was up 70% on a same store basis. We need to adjust to that in our brains, you know.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
We stick around these margins, we'll be happy folks.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah. Yeah.
Josh Chan
Director and Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Yeah. Definitely understood. That's a good problem to have and, congrats, guys.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. One moment for our next question. Our next question comes from Julio Romero from Sidoti & Company. Your line is now open.
Julio Romero
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Sidoti & Company
Thanks. Hey, good morning, guys.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Morning, Julio.
Julio Romero
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Sidoti & Company
Hey, can you maybe talk about the margins you're seeing in construction? Are they trending upward? Are you seeing any fixed cost leverage as that modular business continues to grow?
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
You know, for sure our construction margins, you know, increased the back half of this year into this year. We, you know, there's a lot of multiple reasons for it, but the crux of it is, you know, good job selection with good customers. I got to tell you, we're executing in the field, which is always where the rubber meets the road for me at, you know, a very high level. We really are very grateful to the folks that go out to these jobs every day and the work they're doing. Margins are up and, to me, a lot of it's about the execution that we're getting.
Julio Romero
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Sidoti & Company
Got it. Now, great execution. I'm just curious if there's any kind of fixed cost leverage that you see there as that grows.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Well, you know.
Julio Romero
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Sidoti & Company
As it gets bigger.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
We saw our SG&A obviously dropped from 11.5 to 10.6. I would say we are definitely making investments to accommodate our growth from all sorts of back office sales. With revenue increasing the way it is, it certainly seems like our SG&A can't go up as fast as that. I don't think you'll see worse SG&A leverage over the course of the rest of this year. Now, revenue increases. You know, if we tell you we're gonna be sort of in the mid-teens or more likely in the high teens in revenue increase, and we were in the twenties this quarter, that means it's gonna average down some. I would say maybe we don't get additional leverage, but.
I don't think you'd see additional leverage sequentially, but I think year over year you're gonna see a ton of leverage. I don't even know, that's just a guess, right? The important part is year-over-year, as far as how that math is, the math comes down into what we're doing, you know. I hope you followed that. I think I wasn't very clear in that answer.
Julio Romero
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Sidoti & Company
No, that was good commentary. What's your best guess as to when you see some of this cash flow reversal that's expected?
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Well, our history of getting that right is poor because it keeps waiting, it keeps happening later. I'd say late this year, probably at some point. There is a sense in which, you know, it did flatten because we're gonna show you a slide in our investor presentation. Last quarter, we had a slide in our investor presentation that showed that we had cash flowed $300 million more than we had earned in 2023. You're gonna see at the end of Q1 that on a trailing 12-month basis, we will have cash flowed more than we have earned by $300 million. Here's the thing, so the $300 million didn't go up, right? It didn't go down, but we didn't get in our same store businesses.
Now, we did inherit some advanced cash from our acquisition, especially at Summit. In our same store businesses, we didn't get farther out. I think before you start to give some of it back, the first thing that happens is you stop getting more of it. There were certainly signs in Q1 that we stopped getting more of it. Having said that, we're earning so much money. When I looked at why our cash flow was still so big in Q1, you know, in the past quarters, it's been a lot of earnings and advanced cash. This quarter, it was just a lot of earnings and not giving back advanced cash. There was.
You know, there is signs of flattening out as it literally has to, right? If somebody pays you to do a bunch of welding and electrical work, sooner or later, you gotta go do the welding and electrical work. The welders and the electricians, you're gonna pay them. You're gonna have to pay them. It's a fantastic problem to have. Not really a problem, but it will look like a problem at some point 'cause at some point in the future, our cash flow will be less than our earnings by the amount that it was more than our earnings. You know, it's a high-class problem.
Julio Romero
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Sidoti & Company
Certainly is. Thanks for the color, guys. Appreciate it.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
All right. Thanks, Leo.
Operator
Thank you. One moment for our next question. Our next question comes from Brent Thielman from D.A. Davidson. Your line is now open.
Brent Thielman
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
Hey, thanks. Good morning, guys.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Good morning, Brent.
Brent Thielman
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
I'm gonna ask about margins. Sorry. I guess that you look at this quarter, I mean, just take a step back. Is the margin performance because you're getting paid more generally for what you do, or that you have the perfect mix of projects where you get paid more, or you're just that much more productive in the field?
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
I would say all three. You know, the thing that we really can control on an everyday basis is how we're doing in the field. You know, Brent, you heard this a lot of times, different version of prefabrication. Think that the more work we can do sort of inside a building and ship it to the field, the more productive, safer, the higher quality the work is. We're doing more prefabrication every day. You know, it's a combination of all three for sure, but we really cannot minimize how well we are executing on a per person basis at these job sites, including service. We talk a lot about construction, but our service folks are doing a hell of a job as well.
The other thing you gotta mention is electrical. Like, our electrical margins popped by 600 basis points this quarter. What was amazing about that, we had something like that a year and a half ago where we had an extraordinary gain in the quarter. This was just a mixture of everything good that can happen to a business because they're doing a great job. Our customers really value the ability we have to go out and bring the manpower that's needed to do big jobs. They're allowing us to really help, you know, reward the people so that we can keep doing that. So electrical is mind-blowing. Really amazing quarter. You know, you could say, Well, is that a one-time blip? The answer is, I wouldn't bet against them.
I mean, it's pretty hard to stay at this percentage, but I think they're just gonna. They got a long runway ahead of them of doing well.
Brent Thielman
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
Okay. You know, just looking back, I don't think you guys have ever had a year when EBITDA margins for the rest of the year were below Q1. I know the company in the mix has evolved quite a bit in the last 10 years. I heard your comment, kind of perfect storm of weather both sides. I'm just trying to unpack the reasons why we should be careful in thinking that this is tough to repeat given-
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah, there's one reason. It's our EBITDA on a same store basis was up 70% in Q1. It's pretty hard to well, see that happen and say, "Oh, yeah, there's our new baseline." Right? I understand. I we don't know what's gonna happen, but these margins are, for a Q1, they are extraordinary. Now, do I think we've got extraordinary margins in our future? I do. On a comparable basis, it's a tough comparable. We're about to hit tough comparables from the prior year, and our Q1 was comparable for the ages. We're about to make a lot of money.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
We'll go for it.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah, we'll make as much money as we can, and you can figure out what that means.
Brent Thielman
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
I got an idea. Okay. I just wanted to come back to modular. I mean, I think you're essentially booked in 2024. To what degree do you still have available capacity in 2025 to fill? Are conversations starting at all for 2026?
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
I would say we believe that if we had more capacity, we could sell more than we have capacity for in 2025. We have more of our capacity in 2025 sold than we would have thought was possible. You know, we don't think all of these factors are gonna end by 2026. 2026 is a long. We don't have bookings. You know, we don't have the floor planned for the middle of 2026. You know what I mean? Nobody's doing manpower loading schedules right now for, you know, for the Winter Olympics.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah. That's a long time out.
Brent Thielman
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
Maybe if you could just talk about the progression with new customers in modular. I know you don't wanna talk about name specifics for obvious reasons, but how are you being able to diversify the customer base in that business?
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Things are going great with our second large customer. We like them. They like us. The product they've designed, we think is very, very clever and gonna do a great job for them. You know, we've sold as much as we would have hoped as we could sell by now. As far as diversifying, the thing that keeps us from diversifying is that fantastic customers are willing to buy all of our capacity. Like, we reserve a little bit of that capacity for a lot of long-time pharma customers who really rely on us to do certain things that any other people would have a hard time doing. We have to do that, right, because we owe it to them. In general, so far, those two customers want all we can do, and they've earned first. Really, frankly, they've earned first look and last look. They're great partners.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Absolutely.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
As long as they're good partners, we take, you know, what the market, we do the work. The skills we have are applicable to all kinds of things, right? It's not like in our market, it's always lumpy, and it's always the case that whether there's more of something in any given year. Right now, you know, we're sticking with guys that need what we can do, and they've been great partners, and they've earned our loyalty.
Brent Thielman
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
Yeah.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
They've asked us, "What do we need to do to have all of your capacity?" We've said, "Well, you need to do." They've done it. They've asked us. Last year, they said, "What do you need in order to expand your capacity?" We said, "Look, to be fair to our shareholders, and the risks that we take, and the costs we incur, we need these kind of commitments," and they made them. We're keeping our commitments to them.
Brent Thielman
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
Yeah. Maybe just one last one, guys. I mean, I think it's, you know, obvious that you know, the opportunities in data centers has brought a lot of attention to the company and the stock from investors. You know, clearly, I think it's driving a lot of growth for you. Maybe just your perspective, is that overemphasized relative to, you know, some of the other things moving the needle for your business right now? You know, you talk about manufacturing, industrial capacity.
Bill George
CFO, Comfort Systems USA
Yeah.
Brent Thielman
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
I'd just be curious your thoughts to that.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Well, I mean, I think it's logical that people focus on data centers as, you know, when you and I were touring a couple of weeks ago, it was everybody's favorite topic. You know, if you look at the other stuff we got going on, you know, just take Indianapolis, for example, how much pharma is going on, food. You know, there's a lot of sectors, you know, that are very busy in work that we're good at, whether you're talking about battery plants, food, pharma, hospitals, you know, education, university work is still very strong. I think we're seeing multi-sector activity. I think data centers is gonna get a lot of attention for a while. Those other sectors, we love them. Winning a lot of work in them, and the work's going well.
Brent Thielman
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
Okay. Thanks for taking the questions, guys.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
All right. Thanks, Brent.
Operator
Thank you. I'm showing no further questions. I would now like to turn the call back over to Brian Lane for closing remarks.
Brian Lane
President and CEO, Comfort Systems USA
Okay, Justin. In closing, I really wanna thank our amazing employees once again. We are really grateful for their daily efforts. We do appreciate everyone's interest on the call, you know, in our business. It's great to talk about it and thank you. You know, I'm very optimistic about 2024. We got great customers, we got great people, and you know, really looking forward to how the year pans out and as well as seeing most of you on the road. Probably here pretty sure, pretty soon. Thanks for that too, and hope everyone has a great spring. Thanks, and enjoy your weekend. Thanks, folks.
Operator
This concludes today conference call. Thanks for participating and you may now disconnect.
